speaker: NARRATOR
text: It's 11:59 p.m. Your phone is face down on the nightstand. It buzzes once. You flip it over.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Forty-six new notifications. Normal. Except every single one is stamped tomorrow.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Tomorrow, 7:02 a.m. Mom: Don't forget your lunch. Tomorrow, 10:15 a.m. School alert: Fire drill.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: You go to sleep. At 7:02, a voice comes up the stairs.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: At 10:15, the fire alarm goes off. Exactly on time.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Your name is Maya. You're sixteen. And your phone just showed you tomorrow. So what if your phone showed tomorrow's notifications today?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Here's the rule. Every night at 11:59, tomorrow's notifications land on your lock screen. The time. The sender. The first forty characters. You can't open them. You can't reply. And you'll learn the hard way: tomorrow keeps count.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: One industry study found the average American gets about 46 push notifications a day. You get yours a day early.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Day one. Tomorrow, 8:05 a.m. Mr. Okafor posted: Pop quiz, chapter seven. So tonight, you read chapter seven. Twice.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Here's the real part. Without review, most people forget most of something new within a day. Scientists call it the forgetting curve. You reviewed at eleven p.m. Twenty out of twenty.
